APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWrNED TRANSPORTATION LINES

speakeroldname: Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved:
speechtext: That a sessional committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government be appointed to consider the accounts and estimates and bills relating thereto of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, and Trans-Canada Air Lines, saving always the powers of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public moneys; and that the said committee be empowered to send for persons, papers and records, and to report from time to time, and that, notwithstanding standing order 63, the said committee consist of Messrs. Chevrier, Clark, Coyle, Beaudoin, Belzile, Bourget, Emmerson, Gibson (Comox-Alberni), Harkness, Harris (Grey-Bruce), Harris (Dan-forth), Hazen, Jackman, Lacroix, Lockhart, Maybank, McCulloch (Pictou), Moore, Mutch, Nicholson, Picard, Reid, Shaw.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister what the powers of this committee are to be. When a similar committee was first appointed around the year 1929, it was given the task of going over the budget of the Canadian National Railways. Since that time they have added steamship, ocean and hotel services, and now they are going to add civil aviation. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been invested by this country in the Canadian National Railways, in its ocean and hotel services, and especially in civil aviation services. Unless we solve this civil aviation question aright and have a proper civil aviation policy the British empire will face liquidation. When this committee was first appointed I asked whether the House of Commons was divesting itself of all public control over this great national system of railways, ocean services and hotel services-and now we have aviation services, on which the future of the British empire depends. I asked when this committee was appointed for the first time if

Railways and Shipping Committee
individual members of parliament would have the right to go before it and ask questions, and the minister replied that they would.
I have read the reports of this committee and I fail to see where there has been any proper investigation of the affairs of this railway system. The membership of this committee, like that of other committees, is made up largely of laymen, although there are a few members who know something about transportation. However, hardly anyone who has served on this committee is an outspoken public-ownership man. Many who have served on this committee have had experience in municipal affairs, but I have been unable in other years to find any outstanding supporter of public ownership who has been a member of this committee.
As to the way the committee is conducted, I may say that I have visited the committee dozens of times. The members were all smoking cigars and they seemed to be having a good time. They travel around the country a lot, but I have "failed to find any recommendations made by this committee to the high court of parliament which show that a proper detailed investigation has been made of this great public utility which is so necessary to the building up of this country and the development of its natural resources.
I warn the House of Commons that if this committee is appointed its report will be brought down a day or two before the house closes, with no time to discuss it. There will not be time to examine it as it should be examined. I notice that they are adding the consideration of expenditure relating to civil aviation. They have appointed a board to handle civil aviation. All parliament does if we pass this motion is to divest itself of all authority and hand the whole system over to boards. Who are the officers of the board? Let us look over the list of the permanent officers. Some of them have been promoted to the office of vice-president, but I doubt if they ever had the necessary experience. This is a great public utility.
You can appoint this committee if you like. No doubt it will be appointed, but the investigations by this committee in former years were practically no investigation at all of the system. I have read the reports dozens of times. It reminds me of the war expenditures committee, by which we divested ourselves of control.

Standing order 38 reads:
The following motions are debatable:
Every motion
(a) standing on the order of proceedings for the day, except government notices of motion for the house to go into committee at a later date.
You are quite right, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, we are divesting ourselves of all control over expenditures of this system.
If the hon. member admits that I am right, he should resume his seat.
I have spoken on this motion every year, sir. I have objected to the appointment of this committee which takes from the control of parliament the whole policies of the national railway system.
Order.
I have been generous with the hon. gentleman, and he should resume his seat.

I do not intend to allow this motion to pass without a pro-test from one who has been a public ownership man all his life. I fail to see where the public ownership principle in administration has been carried out by the system.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great diffidence that I rise in view of your ruling a moment ago in connection with freedom in discussing a resolution of this kind to set up a committee. I well recall, and I am sure that Your Honour will recall, that in previous sessions not only have a few moments or a few hours been taken up in debating the setting up of a committee; we have spent as much as three or four days in such a debate. With this explanation, I should like to take two ar three minutes of the time of the house, because this seems to be the only opportunity I may have, -to place upon the record what I think is a well deserved tribute to a group of our Canadian citizens.
Of the contribution which has been made by other branches of our civilian population, none will occupy a greater or more glorious page on Canada's home front history of the war than that of those engaged in the various branches of our transportation services. When I say this I am but reflecting the widespread and general public opinion on this point. But it is not alone on the home front that those in transport service have done their bit. Let me take as only one example those employed by the railway systems of this dominion. It is a proud record to which railwaymen right across Canada may point when it is recorded that almost 43,000 of their number have served in the armed forces of Canada in this war. Taking as a basis the number of employees on both roads at the beginning of the war, more than one out of every four railway workers in Canada enlisted in our armed
*1121

Railways and Shipping Committee
forces. It is doubtful if a better record can be shown by any other branch of our national activity.
While their brothers were fighting for Canada the railway workers at home performed an almost impossible task of transportation. The strain and pressure of war was nowhere felt at home more acutely than by our railway transportation systems. How they mastered the task was little less than a miracle; for in 1938-I would like the house to pay special attention to these figures, because they are next to miraculous-the railways of Canada carried 78 million tons of freight, while in 1944 the freight tonnage had jumped from 78 million tons to 152 million tons. Passenger traffic increases tell a similar story. In 1938 the railways carried 17-J million passengers: in 1944 they carried 54-j million passengers, or more than three times the volume of the last peace time year.
Let us not forget that with all the urgency and all the strain and all the pressure attendant upon war-time operation of our Canadian railways, only seven passengers were killed in Canada through railway accidents in the year 1944. The ratio of those killed and injured in railway accidents, whether passengers or not, is very much lower in 1944 than in the smaller peace-time traffic year of 1938. This is a silent but eloquent tribute to the efficiency of the railways of Canada which needs no elaboration from me.
It will be interesting to hon. members to know, too, that during the last calendar year, 3,100 dining car employees in the two great systems of Canada served en route with notable efficiencs- and service no less than nine million meals. Were time to permit, the story would go on through every branch of transportation activity to show the superb war-time job which was done.
Mr. M. J. COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar).: Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself and my hon. friends writh the tribute that has . just been paid by the hon. member- for Peel (Mr. Graydon) to the work of the men in charge of our transportation systems. Many of us who had to travel from time to time across this country before the war as well as and particularly, during the war, were amazed at the efficiency of the conductors, engineers, sleeping-car porters, dining-car stewards, and those charged with the responsibility of looking after railway offices and providing us with reservations. I am sure that what the ' hon. member for Peel has said is echoed by every member of this house no matter where he sits.
But what I really rose to do was to support the appointment of this committee, and I do so because of the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). It would be a mistake if at any time we in this House of Commons, elected in a legislative capacity, were called upon to try to operate an economic utility owned by the country. The method we have adopted in Canada of establishing government-owned corporations which by statute are free from active interference on the part of members of this House of Commons is the sane and proper method of handling publicly-owned institutions. The members who are elected to this house have no right, in my opinion, to interfere with the internal management of organizations such as this, and it is our duty to see to it that politics, in the sense in which we use the term in this chamber, does not enter into the running of our railways or our broadcasting system or any other publicly-owned utility which we have established or may establish in the future. As time passes, more and more of these' great economic organizations will come under the ownership and control of the people, and they should be operated entirely apart from the legislative arm; for the two arms, legislative and economic, are quite distinct. As long as we have the right to investigate the proceedings of these organizations to see that they give the people service and do a good job, our responsibility in connection with them as elected members of this house ends. As a warm supporter of the social ownership of industry I believe that in setting up these corporations under public ownership and control, under a statute of this parliament, and making them responsible to parliament through a committee of the house, we are doing what is the only sane thing to do. It is with pleasure, therefore, that I concur in the appointment of this committee.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Mr. Speaker, before this motion passes I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Every province is supposed to be interested in this committee and every province is supposed to have a representative on it. I notice that eight provinces are represented on the committee, but Prince Edward Island-again -we come back to Prince Edward Island-is not. We from Prince, Edward Island are interested in this railway, and I would like to ask the Minister of Transport why that province is not represented on the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) as well as the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Cold-



Railways and Shipping Committe*
well), for the tribute which they have just paid to the transportation workers in Canada during the war years. The tribute that each of them has paid is a well-deserved one, and unquestionably the service which these workers have rendered should be referred to in this house. When I made a statement in the house some two or three weeks ago in reference to the extension of an order in council on travel, I paid a tribute to the work being done by the railway and transportation workers across Canada. I think I should add a word now as to what is being done by the railways in the repatriation of our troops from overseas. I am sure the house will agree that what was done in that respect could not have been, better done.
The leader of the C.C.F. party a moment ago pointed to a very important feature in the setting up of this committee, namely, that parliament should retain the right to see that the internal management of the railways is not interfered with, and the proper way to make sure of that is by the appointment of a committee such as this. It strikes me that the setting up of this committee-I know the house will agree, and the motion is in exactly the' same form as in previous years-will ensure the purpose for which it is being established.

subtopic: SIXTEEN PER CENT INCOME TAX ABATEMENT- DEDUCTION AT THE SOURCE

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition). I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, who I understand is the acting Minister of Finance. My question is meant to clear up certain confusion which has arisen in respect of the budget proposal to abate the income tax levy by 16 per cent. To make clear my question let me read from the statement of the Minister of Finance in presenting his budget. He said at page 1006 of Hansard:
I think it wise therefore to recommend an interim measure of prompt and unquestionable relief. It is proposed that the tax levy shall be abated by 16 per cent dating from October 1, 1945. This abatement of 16 per cent will be applied to the current tax deductions at the source just as soon as the necessary change can be made. Since the change is applicable from October 1,. the abatement on the whole tax liability for 1945 will amount to 4 per cent. For a full year, the abatement will be 16 per cent of the tax liability.
This is an interim measure to be applied immediately and to continue until it is possible to combine further abatement with a thorough overhaul of the whole rate structure of the personal income tax.
As a result of that statement taxpayers were led to believe that the abatement would apply in respect of the current month's tax deductions at the- source. However, on Saturday morning, Mr. Fraser Elliott, deputy minister, taxation division, national revenue department, in a statement reported in the press, in apparent direct contradiction of the minister, said that the policy would not apply to tax deductions at the source until January 1, 1946. His statement as reported is as follows:
Employers will continue to use the present existing tables of tax deductions until the end of this calendar year without any change. Thus employees will then have paid substantially 100 per cent of their tax liability on the pay-as-you-earn basis, and the tax reduction provided by the present budget for 1945 will mean that they will have less to pay at the time of filing their * returns on or before April 30.
My question is this: would the minister inform the house whether the statement of the minister in his budget speech is correct, or whether the statement of the deputy minister of the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue is correct?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) : Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Minister of Finance as reported at page 1006 of Hansard which has just been read by the leader of the opposition correctly set forth

Taxation
the intention of the government in the budget proposals which were put before the house by the Minister of Finance on Friday night. It will be noted that in that statement the minister said that the abatement of 16 per cent will be applied to all current tax deductions at the source just as soon as the necessary change can be made. As a matter of fact the deductions at the source are made in accordance with tables which have been prepared and authorized by order in council as regulations for the collection of the income tax, and the commissioner of income tax would have no authority to depart from what is prescribed by the order in council and the tables until some change is made in the regulations.
Though it is always declared in budget proposals that it is intended when the proper legislation is enacted that it will be retroactive to a certain date, it is not in fact legislation until it has passed through the houses of parliament and received the royal assent. Because of that, the commissioner of taxation apparently felt that it would be more convenient, and would make in fact no difference to each ratepayer or each employer, if deductions continued to be made according to the same table to the end of the year, because these deductions are calculated to represent only ninety-five per cent of the liability; in fact one could go on making to the end of the year deductions at the same rate, and the only consequence would be that the ratepayer wTould not have as much as five per cent to pay to satisfy the whole of his tax liability. There have been however a large number of representations and protestations made against this proposal or this suggestion of the commissioner of income tax, that though the Minister of Finance had not said from what date a change in the amount to be deducted might be made, he had said that it would be effective as soon as the necessary change can be made.

He said it would apply immediately.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, it would apply and it does apply, and both the minister and the commissioner intend that it shall in fact affect the amount of tax to be paid. The only question is whether it will be deducted at the source or whether it is something that a man will have to pay after he gets it- which he will have to return to the tax gatherer after he has received it from his employer. There have been a number of protestations that, though it does not affect in any way the liability of the taxpayer, the amount of deductions should be reduced at 47696-711
once by 16 per cent. It is intended at the earliest possible moment, because of the apparent psychological effect of maintaining the deduction at the old rate, to recommend to His Excellency a modification in the order in council, under which employers will be authorized to reduce their deductions immediately by 16 per cent without issuing the new table, because it would take some considerable time to calculate and print the new table and get it into the hands of every employer. But representations have been made that many employers are willing to have their pay clerks make the calculation, and the intention is to recommend to His Excellency an immediate modification of the regulation which will be authority, until such time as parliament has dealt with the recommendations of the Minister of Finance, to the employers to reduce their reductions by the 16 per cent. I hope to-morrow to be able to lay on the table of the house, if His Excellency will be pleased to approve it, an order making that change in the regulations.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been the custom in past sessions in presenting the defence estimates to give a brief operational summary as to what has taken place since the
last report was presented. I should like to follow that course to-day, probably for the last time.
Some hon. members will recall that at the last session I reviewed the operations of our forces from D-day to the beginning of March, at which time the German army had been swept clear from the west bank of the Rhine and north of the Moselle river. Following the clean-up of the west bank of the Rhine the Canadian forces were regrouped for the initial attack across the Rhine. Our forces participated in the crossings of the Rhine that started on March 23, and once again were on the left flank of the assault that was to end in the final defeat of the German armies. The Canadian paratroop battalion was also with the British airborne division that was dropped across the Rhine on the same day. Meanwhile the first Canadian corps was moving from Italy to northwest Europe and during March its units took over a sector on the extreme left of the long allied line. With the reversion of the second corps to the command of the first Canadian, army on the first day of April, all the units of the Canadian Army were fighting together for the first time in its history.
Following the initial crossing and consolidation of the bridgehead across the Rhine, the Canadian army was given the task of clearing Holland. These operations may be broken down into two phases, the first consisting of the initial breaking of the hard crust of resistance and the sealing off of northwestern Holland, and the second being the rapid advances and clearing of northeastern Holland followed by the turn eastwards into Germany to invest the Emden and Wilhelmshaven pocket.
In the first phase our forces attacked from the Nijmegen-Emmerich sector northwestwards, and by April 19 they had reached the shores of the Zuider Zee, thus permanently sealing off the enemy forces caught in southwestern Holland. The first corps turned westwards to deal with this trapped enemy force and ran into stiff opposition, but to the north in Holland resistance was quickly broken. By the middle of April the second corps had reached the north coast of Holland on the Ems estuary and the Kusten canal further east in Germany.
During the second phase, northeast Holland was quickly cleared by our forces against light opposition. On the right very strong opposition was met along the Kusten canal. Similarly the first corps, working slowly into western Holland, also came up against stiff resistance. By the end of the month a truce was arranged to allow food convoys to enter this part of Holland to relieve conditions of extreme food
Demobilization-Army

shortages among the Dutch civilians, and active operations were not again resumed in this sector.
To the north in Germany a bridgehead was established over the Kusten canal on the 17th of April which was expanding northwards into the Emden-Wilhelmshaven peninsula, when the German forces in. northwest Germany and Holland surrendered unconditionally on the 5th of May.
It was fitting that the surrender of the remaining German forces in the Netherlands should be made to a Canadian commander, since our forces played such an important part in the liberation of the territory of this gallant ally. The surrender of all the German forces in the Netherlands, naval and air as well as army, was made by Colonel-General Johannes Blaskowitz to Lieutenant-General Foulkes, then commanding the first Canadian corps and now chief of the general staff. The number of German forces surrendered in the Netherlands was over 185,000.
Before leaving this brief review of the active operations of our forces, may I point out that in the ten months of continuous fighting since D-day the Canadian Army, always fighting on the left and vital-if less spectacular-flank of the allied armies, over the most difficult country, encountered and defeated no fewer than fifty-nine German divisions.
Immediately following the capitulation, our forces began to make their way into western Holland, where they were received with enthusiasm by the civilian papulation. The Canadian Army was then faced with the difficult task of disarming a. greatly superior force of the enemy; the organization and relief of the large civilian population, hungry, and excited by'the sudden turn of events, and the co-ordination of the underground' forces, who were armed and eager to deal with the defeated enemy. This whole operation was accomplished without incident, and is greatly to the credit of the commanders and troops concerned.
The concentration and move out of Holland of the German 25th army was supervised and controlled by our forced, and this difficult undertaking was practically completed by the 15th of June. Meanwhile it was necessary to set up an effective military government in the area of Germany under Canadian command, to restore order in the Netherlands as well as in German territory, to prevent the spread of disease and to develop the essential services and the. welfare of the civilian population. Added to these, problems was the intricate question of the provision for handling the

large numbers of prisoners of war and displaced persona who were migrating in large numbers over the area controlled by our forces. All these measures were carried, out in the most efficient and satisfactory manner, so that by the. 14th of June General Crerar's responsibility for military government in the German area was concluded and handed over to the occupational district corps command, and by the 30th of June the Dutch authorities were able to resume their functions after the long usurpation by the Germans.
During this time the important problems of reallocation and repatriation of the army's man-power were receiving attention, and all ranks were at once informed of the requirements for the Pacific war and for the army of occupation. On the 4th of July a composite batallion, made up of three different units and accompanied by a band, entered Berlin for a tour of duty of several weeks under command of headquarters of the British troops in Berlin. Machinery was set up in the Netherlands for the organization of the Canadian Army occupation force and for the early return of volunteers for the far east and of long service personnel.
The organization of the occupation force under command of Major-General C. Vokes was completed rapidly, and this force moved into Germany between the 5th and 12th of July to take up its occupation duties in the Emden-Wilhelmshaven area under command of the British 30th corps district.
Preparations were made for the immediate dispatch to United Kingdom repatriation depots of the volunteers for the Pacific force. This force was being organized in Canada as a division to operate against Japan under command of United States forces. It was therefore necessary to reorganize and to reequip this force along United States lines, although the uniforms were to have been Canadian. As the units were formed and the volunteers were returned from the army overseas, they were concentrated in camps across Canada, together with the necessary reinforcements that it was proposed should move with the force. The units of this force with its reinforcements, after their organization and preliminary training, were to have moved to Camp Breckenridge in Kentucky to complete its organization and training under United States army command. At the time of the capitulation of Japan, this force was still in Canada and was accordingly disbanded.
That, Mr. Chairman, is briefly the record of the information available since the last report I gave the house at the previous session early in April.

Demobilization-Army
Before discussing the problem of demobilization and outlining plans for the future, I should like to give the committee a short statistical resume of the development of the Canadian Army during the war.
In round figures one million men and forty-five thousand women have served in the armed forces since the outbreak of the war. This exceeds by more than 60 per cent the
620.000	who served in the war of 1914-18.
Enlistments and enrolments for the army
alone number some 730,000 including 25,000 women. Of the total, 630,000 were volunteers while 100,000 men served under the provision of the National Resources Mobilization Act. In all, 158,000 men entered the army under the National Resources Mobilization Act, but over 57,000 of these enlisted for general service in the army. In addition nearly 6,000 more transferred to the navy or air force as volunteers. I am dealing, of course, in round figures.
Of the 730,000 who have served in the army,
45.000	served in commissioned ranks. Of this number, 26,000 were appointed from the reserve army or direct from civilian life and
19.000	from the ranks. However, excluding doctors, dentists, chaplains and nurses who are all appointed direct to 'Commissioned ranks, over half of the remaining officers received their promotion from the ranks of the active army.
Until March, 1944, the strength of the army grew more or less continuously, reaching a total of 495,000 all ranks at that time. From that date forward total casualties and discharges were about equal to the numbers enlisting or being enrolled and the strength of the armj' remained almost constant until V-E day.
Over 370,000 all ranks served in the European zone-the highest strength at any one time being over 280,000. This strength was reached during the last few months before V-E day.
The maximum strength in Canada at any one time was 265,000 in May, 1943. This does not include those in so-called adjacent territories. This maximum strength was reached at a time when it was necessary to have comparatively large operational forces in Canada for the protection of our coasts as well as to have a large number in training for the completion of the army overseas and for reinforcements to maintain it. From May, 1943, forward, the strength of the army in Canada decreased because of the disbandment of various formations as the strategic situation improved and the dispatch overseas of units and reinforcements for the first Canadian army.
In addition to the troops in Canada, we had operational units in Alaska and in the islands of the Atlantic. At one time in November, 1943, we had over 14,000 troops in these areas, but this number decreased as it became more and more apparent that the enemy would not be able to bring an attack to bear in these regions.
Up to 30 September last, the total number of casualties reported was 80,530 including
22,553	fatal casualties. We may be thankful that the casualties in this war were so much lighter than in the war of 1914-18, when nearly 60,000 soldiers lost their lives, and the total casualties numbered nearly 200,000 The 80,530 include, besides the 22,553 fatal casualties, 51,487 wounded, 6,435 prisoners of war and 55 currently listed as missing.
There were 505 who died while prisoners of war. In the over-all casualty figures which I have given, these have been included in the fatal casualties rather than among the prisoners of war.	-
The grand total of 80,530 is made up of 76,514 casualties in the European zone, 1,990 in the Asiatic zone and 2,026 in the western hemisphere. The latter is made up of deaths from natural causes as well as from accidents in training, and the like.
In the total are included 6,071 men who were reported as casualties on two occasions, 492 on three occasions, 27 on four occasions, while two were wounded on five occasions. These are included two, three, four or five times as the case may be, in the total of 80,530 which I mentioned.
The two hardy young men, both born in 1919, who were wounded on five occasions each, seem to have had little respect for German ammunition, for one man remained on duty on two of the occasions on which he was wounded, while the other remained on duty on three of the five occasions. Both these young men have recovered from their wounds; one is still overseas at latest report, while the other returned to Canada in May of this year, and was discharged on grounds of long service in July. I might mention that one served with the composite American Canadian force, known as the special service battalion, while the other was with the good old Princess Patricia's Canadian light infantry.
I suppose that every soldier serving overseas tries to bring back with him some souvenir from the battlefield or from the places of interest he visited. There is one variety of prize of which I feel I should make special mention. I mentioned this a day or two ago. I refer to some 32,000 war brides from the British isles, along with 16,500 children. Both those figures are constantly increasing. Five

Demobilization-Army

thousand army brides and 3,500 children had been brought to Canada up to V-E day, while another 7,000 wives and 4,600 children came between V-E day and the end of August. At that time there were 20,000 wives and 8,400 children still in the United Kingdom. These will be brought out to their new homes as rapidly as shipping will permit, although, at the present time, priority is being given to the returning soldiers.
In what I have just said I have tried to outline broadly the more important figures as to strengths, and the like. I shall now try to give the committee a little more detail of what has happened since V-E day.
At that time, the strength of the army was a little more than 490,000, over 280,000 of these in the European zone. Plans at that time called for the immediate formation of the Canadian Army Pacific force and the Canadian Army occupation force. In addition, attention had to be directed to the repatriation of other soldiers and to the demobilization of personnel not required for those forces or the continuing administration and training establishments.
A total of 83,370 volunteered for service with the Canadian Army, Pacific force, 37.304 among personnel serving in the European zone and 46.066 from personnel serving in Canada and adjacent territories. There were 8,253 women included in these totals. The number repatriated from Europe for the Pacific force was approximately 25,000.
Following the defeat of Japan, and the decision that Canada's share in occupational duties, would, in so far as the army was concerned, be confined to the European zone, the Canadian Army Pacific force was disbanded. The personnel of the force were reallocated to other duties, or if eligible for and desiring discharge, were put into the demobilization stream.
The occupation force in Germany consisting of a reformed third Canadian division and certain ancillary troops, numbered on the 30th of September, 1945, 21,549 all ranks. This included 6,777 personnel who volunteered for this duty, the remainder being detailed.
Already 111.000 men of the army have returned to Canada from the European zone since V-E day, leaving fewer than 175,000 there at the present time. The number repatriated up to the present has been somewhat in excess of our expectations as announced in July last by my predecessor.
Although I must speak with the greatest caution because there are so many demands for shipping for troops of all the united nations in the various parts of the. world, I may say that if present plans mature all of 
the army overseas, with the exception of the occupation force and necessary staffs in England, should be repatriated by March or April 1946.
May I at this point appeal to the press to refrain from over-optimistic comments on our repatriation programme. I know it has not been intentional, but there has been a certain idea allowed to get abroad when we have made announcements that additional shipping has been obtained that we can get so many men home by Christmas or so many men home by a certain date. The department is cautious, and I am most cautious about making predictions. The one which I have just given to the committee represents the best, view before us, that is to say, that we shall be able to get all our boys back, with the exception of those in the occupation forces and necessary staff, by late March or April, 1946.
Any mathematical calculations based upon the size of ships that may be allocated to us are apt to be misleading, so I appeal to those who may be discussing these matters to refrain from over-optimistic predictions as to what, may result. I have a most vivid recollection of my own experience sitting in England from November, 1918 to June, 1919, and hearing about other people going home.
I thought I had been forgotten; I thought that shipping had been allocated to everybody but to the Canadians to get them back home.
I know when men are so far away as these men are it is unfortunate if unauthorized and perhaps over-optimistic statements are issued as to what the prospects are. The prospects are good because we are ahead of our expectations as announced last July. I hope that we shall at least maintain that, and perhaps improve it. I do not. want to say that we will improve it until I know definitely that we are going to be able to do it.
Since V-E day the numbers being discharged have increased rapidly month by month, reaching 34,000 for the month of September. I think the best day we have had was last Friday, -when something like 1,950 were discharged and some 500 put. out on extended leave. We are running at the rate of approximately 2,500 for discharges and extended leave. The total discharged from V-E day to date is just over 100,000. Incidentally, I might mention that a reduction in strength of 100,000 corresponds to a saving of about $12,000,000 a month in day-to-day costs for pay and allowances, messing, quarters, clothing and the like.
In addition, the number on extended leave has been increased from 10,000 on V-E day to over 20,000 at the present time.

Demobilization-Army
Although I have already dealt with the matter briefly in the debate on the address I think that perhaps the committee would like to have a somewhat more comprehensive statement of the principles upon which the process of demobilizing the Canadian army is being carried out. There are in this process three main aspects each of which involves its own distinct considerations. I shall refer only to the aspects of repatriation, which is the return to Canada of troops who have been serving overseas, and of discharge, which is the return of the individual to civil life. The third aspect, which is rehabilitation, is not within the army ambit, but comes under the administration of my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
The common principle underlying the whole scheme of demobilization has always been, and in future, will continue to be th^t subject to the exigencies of the service and to the national interests, the personnel with the longest and hardest service should be given first opportunity to return to civil life. However, the loose description of this as a policy of "first in-first out" is somewhat misleading, as it ignores the two essential qualifications to which the main principle has always been subject.' It is inevitable that there should occasionally occur some combination of circumstances or unusual conditions wherein a general policy becomes inapplicable, or wherein an exception must be made. In such an event the interests of Canada or of the majority of personnel directly concerned must, in the final instance, receive' preference over the single person or minor group affected. The circumstances must always be viewed as a whole-and judgment cannot be correctly passed in the light of a single factor or isolated incident.
It is, of course, highly essential to maintain the effective administration, welfare and discipline of the troops still awaiting repatriation or discharge and where this depends upon the particular ability or experience of any individuals, they must continue to be retained for a further period even though they might nominally be eligible, and presumably entitled, to repatriation or discharge. The commander in the field is the only man who can judge all the circumstances as a whole and properly decide whether, in a particular instance, the eligibility and wishes of the individual must give way to the greater needs of the army as represented by the mass of other servicemen in that formation or area in order to adequately supervise the remaining troops and take care of their material needs by experienced tradesmen and specialists.	[DOT]
47696-72J
The corollary of such a policy is that "freezing" of personnel should be kept to the minimum, and constant reviews made to release such personnel as soon as their services can be dispensed with or a replacement trained and made available. Some mistakes will be inevitable, but I am confident that the respective commanders in the field, whether in formation or in unit, by whom decisions in respect of individuals have to be made, will use their judgment in a capable, fair and impartial way.
Similarly, it may have to be determined by the government, on taking all circumstances into account, that a variation or exception to the basic principle is requisite in the national interest for purposes such as carrying on vital industries or developing basic resources to create added employment, easing the critical housing shortage, lessening the gap in higher education caused by the war, or meeting the man-power shortage in certain primary industries. It is a cardinal principle, however, that the soldier still overseas awaiting his turn for repatriation and discharge should not be prejudiced in obtaining employment through any such variation or exception.
The individual point score system is the means of giving expression to the basic principle that I have been discussing but this, being a relative measurement of service, does not, of itself, constitute an absolute right to discharge: it. must be applied with due regard to the other qualifying factors which I have just mentioned as being inherent in the process of demobilization.
As all members of the committee, I think, are aware, the point score is determined by allotting three points for each month of service overseas and two points for each month of service in Canada. To the total of these, a further 20 per cent is added where the individual has marital status as a married man, a widower or a divorced man with a dependent child. The scoring is effective over the period from September 10, 1939, until the selected datum date, March 31, 1945
Point scores are being used as a guide in determining priorities for repatriation as well as priorities for discharge, but these are two separate and distinct operations. The conditions and relative interests involved by one are not the same in extent and degree as those which concern the other. Therefore, the considerations which necessitate and justify an accelerated discharge in advance of the normal priority by score are applicable only in respect of discharge and would not ordinarily carry any entitlement to accelerated repatriation from overseas. The only
Demobilization-Army

exceptions at present are cases of accelerated repatriation for return of "key" men in essential industry or for discharge on compassionate grounds. On the other hand, although a wide range of point scores may be possessed by personnel who have been returned to Canada as a unit, they will be required to await discharge here according to their relative scores or other qualifications for release.
The' regulations governing discharge are established and administered by National Defence headquarters in conformity with the broad policies and objects determined by the government. But while the broad principles in respect of repatriation are first submitted for approval by the government and National Defence headquarters as appropriate, the operative regulations are developed through Canadian military headquarters at London, and their detailed application is carried out by Canadian military headquarters and by headquarters Canadian forces Netherlands through their local commanders in the field. They are best in a position- to evaluate all the local circumstances as well as individual characteristics and experience when making final decision as to administrative needs or as to what individual may necessarily have to be retained beyond his normal expectation.
The basic plan for repatriation is, I believe, sound and straightforward, but its detailed application has involved most careful study and planning. The primary concern has been to return to Canada as soon as possible those men who had been separated from their homes and families for many long years. But precedence had necessarily to be given to the operational need of immediately moving the Canadian Army Pacific force volunteers to this country for their inclusion with the American force that was destined for the Pacific.
The limited shipping resources made it inevitable that some months must pass before the bulk of Canadian troops could be returned home and this necessitated continuation of their organization as formations and units overseas in order to adequately administer and maintain the troops during their period of waiting. Alternatively, hardship, inconvenience or discomfort might well result fiom breakdown of an improvised or sketchy organization. Consideration also had to be given to the interest in Canada in the return of units having a militia affiliation and territorial identity so that the invaluable provincial and community interest in such units would be recognized and formation of a strong peace-time militia assisted.

Thus it was decided in principle that following the return of men with very long service, which was to be carried out at far as feasible, the men with relatively shorter service should return by units or unit drafts in the order in which their original formations proceeded overseas, i.e., First Canadian Division, Second Canadian Division, Third Canadian Division, Fifth Armoured Division and Fourth Armoured Division. This repatriation plan, and the basis for point scoring, were duly notified to all ranks overseas by the pamphlet "After Victory in Europe" issued to them immediately following V-E day. I suppose that the committee has seen this pamphlet, which was issued by General Crerar early in May.
Exact adherence to the descending order of point scores in return of personnel would naturally result in depletion of officers both commissioned and non-commissioned, at a more rapid rate than would apply to private soldiers for, on the average, officers would have longer service. No army can function effectively without an adequate proportion of commissioned and non-commissioned officers, and accordingly a certain number of them proportionate to the total strength must be retained despite their length of service.
Moreover, the services necessary for maintenance of the health and comfort of the troops involve retention of a proper proportion of certain specialists or tradesmen, such as cooks, clerks, medical orderlies, etc. In fact, some tradesmen, such as clerks for instance, are required in even greater numbers than normal when troops are being demobilized owing to the great increase in documentation that is involved.
The exact stage at which the further return of individuals, according to height of point score, would begin to seriously affect organization and administration of the remaining troops, had to be determined by the commander in the field and it was with all these considerations in mind that General Crerar was finally obliged to decide that personnel with point scores below fifty would be retained for duty with the occupation force, and that for personnel with scores between 50 and 149 points, return would be carried out by units according to their respective formations. That movement is now in progress, and the majority of units of first Canadian division are now home.
With reduction not only in total numbers of personnel, but also in the numbers of units being maintained overseas, it becomes possible to correspondingly reduce the extent, though not the degree, of services provided. Thus it becomes possible, by interposting, to progres-

Demobilization-Jirmy
sively take out the next higher point score men from among the remaining units and return them in what we call Canada drafts between the moves of the divisions. This works out a balance between individuals and units with fairness to each of them.
Current moves, which are now virtually completed, have been, first, personnel with a point score of 150 and over who could be spared repatriated in Canada drafts, and second, units of the 1st Division group.
Future moves as at present planned are:
1.	Canada drafts made up of personnel with 130 points and over who can be spared.
2. Units of 2nd Division group, followed by more Canada drafts made up of personnel with point score down to 110.
3.	Units of 3rd Division group, followed by more Canada drafts with point score down to 90.
4. Units of 5th Division group and 4th Division group, followed by remaining personnel from headquarters and repatriation depots.
I should mention here that units of divisions moving as such will return to Canada with all personnel on strength at time of moving having a score of 50 points or over. Those with a score of less than 50 points will remain for further duty.
The units of army troops will be disbanded as the administrative requirements of the remaining formations permit and their services are no longer required. Individuals who can be spared will be repatriated in Canada drafts appropriate to their point score.
This repatriation plan which I have briefly outlined was first announced by General ' Crerar early in May and has also been explained in detail to the overseas troops by means of a pamphlet recently issued by Lieutenant-General Simonds, Commander of the Canadian forces in the Netherlands.
On V-E day there were of course more men with high point scores overseas than there were in Canada, but the shipping situation imposed a restriction on the number of them that could become available in Canada for early discharge. The sudden arrival of V-J day brought a great demand in Canada for man-power to assist in reconversion and development of industry. In these circumstances, it would obviously not be in the national interest to maintain a considerable number of soldiers in idleness in Canada, to await the return for discharge of slightly higher point score personnel from overseas.
It was therefore decided that demobilization of some of the troops in Canada had to be carried out, but in so doing, the just claims of the overseas troops to priority in obtaining employment must be protected.
The classes now made eligible for discharge from those serving in Canada have therefore been restricted as far as possible to groups who would not compete for employment, that is, students or personnel returning to jobs in which they are entitled to be reinstated.
Discharge may now be obtained, subject to the needs of the service, on point score alone if it is 120 points or over (as of March 31, 1945) which means that even if the individual has served Tn Canada only, he must have entered the army before March 1941 if married, and before May 1940 if single. I do not think that anyone should object to the discharge of a man who has served four and a half years.
In the case of men who are eligible for release to return to their former civil employment, or to work of national importance upon application by the employer through the appropriate industrial selection and release committee, they are not granted a full discharge unless they have a score within 20 points of the current qualifying score which means at present that they must have at least 100 points. If they have a lesser score they are only given extended leave without pay and allowances and are not eligible for discharge until their point score is as great as the current qualifying limit which at present is 120 points.
Apart from the other normal grounds for discharge which have always existed during the war, a service man is now entitled to a discharge: (i) if he has been wounded, is a liberated prisoner of war or has served more than two years overseas; (ii) if he has served in the war 1914-1918; (iii) if he has attained 42 years of age; (iv) if he had not attained 19 years of age by V-J day; (v) if he was one of the very few who on V-J day were still in district depot awaiting transfer to a training unit.
Resumption of university .or equivalent higher education has also been made a basis for immediate discharge and while this may be extended to a limited degree with respect to secondary schools, it does not include resumption of technical or business training. The reason for this is fairly obvious: while the war caused a complete gap for almost six years in university training, there has not been the same material diminution in secondary education and, taking into account the personnel trained in the army or in war plants, there has even likely been an increase, in trades or technically trained people as a result of the war.

la so far as the reserve army is concerned, it is to be organized as a force of six divisions with supporting armoured elements and selected corps and army troops for an army of two corps. In addition, the reserve army will include our operational coast and anti-aircraft . artillery units and supporting services necessary for the static defence of the country.
So far as the plans have so far progressed, service in the reserve army will be on a parttime basis, and it is intended that the present three-year term of engagement will be continued. Adequate equipment of the latest type will be available on a generous scale to ensure that the training of the reserve army is realistic and interesting. It is intended to assist commanding officers of reserve army units in the training and administration of their personnel by providing for each unit full time (active force) officers and other ranks on an' adequate scale.
Those who are familiar with the existing organization of the reserve army will appreciate that the new proposals follow generally the pattern of its present organization and are consistent with the arrangement of our active force during the war. A rearrangement of
units will be necessary in order to secure the numbers and types required in the light of modern operational experience. I may add that it is intended to consult the representatives of the various defence associations, whose cooperation and assistance have been of great value to the department in the past, before the resulting changes in the present composition of the reserve army are finally decided.
I hope that many of those who have seen service in the present war will continue that service in the reserve army so that this important force which will form the background of any possible future military endeavour will, as far as possible, be led by commissioned and non-commissioned officers who have gained field experience in the active army under conditions of modern warfare.

speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot at the moment. The strength of six divisions plus would indicate that it would be somewhere in the vicinity of 130,000 to 150,000 men, with supporting troops which might be somewhat substantially in excess of that. Before giving a definite answer I would want to discuss it with the chief of the general staff to see what his views are as to that. The general picture, as I have indicated, is a force of six divisions plus the usual headquarters staff and supporting troops.
The committee will recall that lists of operational awards and honours have been submitted previously. With those which I have presented to-day, the total is 5,765. Included in the list are the names of three members of the army who received the Victoria Cross. I regret to say that one of these, Sergeant Aubrey Cosens, of the Queen's Own Rifles of Canada, was killed in action and the cross was awarded posthumously. The other two, Major Frederick Albert Tilston of the Essex Scottish and Corporal Frederick George Topham of the first Canadian parachute battalion, happily survived and have been repatriated.
The citations in the cases of Sergeant Cosens and Captain Tilston appeared in the Canada Gazette of May 26, 1945, and in the case of Corporal Topham in the Gazette of August 4, 1945. I shall read them, Mr. Chairman, in order that they may be on Hansard.
First, that of Sergeant Cosens reads as follows:
The king has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the Victoria Cross (posthumously) to:
B.46495 Sergeant Aubrey Cosens, the Queen's Own Rifles of Canada
In Holland on the night of February 25-26, 1945, the first battalion the Queen's Own Rifles of Canada launched an attack on the hamlet of Mooshof to capture ground which was considered essential for the successful development of future operations.
Sergeant Cosens platoon with two tanks in support attacked enemy strong-points in three farm buildings but were twice beaten back by fanatical enemy resistance and then fiercely counter-attacked during which time the platoon suffered heavy casualties and the platoon commander was killed.
Sergeant Cosens at once assumed command of the only other four survivors of his platoon whom he placed in a position to give him covering fire while he himself ran across open ground under heavy mortar and shell fire to
Demobilization-Army

the one remaining tank where, regardless of danger, he took up an exposed place in front ot the turret and directed his fire.
After a further enemy counter-attack had been repulsed, Sergeant Cosens ordered the tank to attack the farm building while the four survivors of his platoon followed in close support. After the tank had rammed the first building he entered alone killing several of the defenders and taking the rest prisoners.
Single-handed he then entered the second and third buildings and perosnally killed or captured all the occupants although under intense machine gun and small arm fire.
Just after the successful reduction of these important enemy strong-points Sergeant Cosens was shot through the head by an enemy sniper and died almost instantly.
The outstanding gallantry, initiative and determined leadership of the brave N.C.O. who himself killed at least twenty of the enemy and took an equal number of prisoners resulted in the capture of a position which was vital to the success of the future operations of the brigade.
The second, the citation of Major Frederick Albert Tilston, reads as follows:
The king has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the Victoria Cross to:
Captain (Acting Major) Frederick Albert Tilston,
the Essex Scottish.
The second Canadian division had been given the task of breaking through the strongly fortified Hochwald forest defence line which covered Xanten, the last German bastion west of the Rhine protecting the vital Wesel bridge escape route.
The Essex Scottish regiment was ordered to breach the defence line northwest of Udem and to clear the northern half of the forest through which the balance of the brigade would pass.
At 0715 hours on first March, 1945, the attack was launched but due to the softness of the ground it was found impossible to support the attack by tanks as had been planned.
Across approximately 500 yards of flat open country in face of intense enemy fire Major Tilston personally led his company in the attack keeping dangerously close to our own bursting shells in order to get the maximum cover from the barrage. Though wounded in the head, he continued to lead his men forward through a belt of wire ten feet in depth to the enemy trenches shouting orders and encouragement and using his sten gun with great effect. When the platoon on the left came under heavy fire from an enemy machine gun post, he dashed forward personally and silenced it with a grenade. He was first to reach the enemy position and take the first prisoner.
Determined tq maintain the momentum of the attack he ordered the reserve platoon to mop up these positions and with outstanding gallantry pressed on with his main force to the second line of enemy defences which were on the edge of the woods.
As he approached the woods he was severely wounded in the hip and fell to the ground. Shouting to his men to carry on without him and urging them to get into the wood he struggled to his feet and rejoined them as they reached the trenches on their objective. Here an elaborate system of underground dugouts and trenches was manned in considerable fMr. Abbott.]
strength and vicious hand to hand fighting followed. Despite his wounds, Major Tilston's unyielding will to close with the enemy was a magnificent inspiration to his men as' he led them in systematically clearing the trenches of the fiercely resisting enemy. In this fighting two German company headquarters were overrun and many casualties were inflicted on the fanatical defenders.
Such had been the grimness of the fighting and so savage the enemy resistance that the company was now reduced to only twenty-six men, one-quarter of its original strength. Before consolidation could be completed the enemy counter-attacked repeatedly supported by a hail of mortar and machine gun fire from the open flank. Major Tilston moved in the open from platoon to platoon quickly organizing their defence and directing fire against the advancing enemy. The enemy attacks penetrated so close to the positions that grenades were thrown into the trenches held by his troops but this officer by personal contact, unshakeable confidence and unquenchable enthusiasm so inspired his men that they held firm against great odds.
When the supply of ammunition became a serious problem he repeatedly crossed the bullet swept ground to the company on his right flank to carry grenades, rifle and bren ammunition to his troops and replaced a damaged wireless set to reestablish communications with battalion headquarters. He made at least six of these hazardous trips each time crossing a road which was dominated by intense fire from numerous well-sited enemy machine gun posts.
On his last trip he was wounded for the third time, this time in the leg. He was found in a shell crater beside the road. Although very seriously wounded and barely conscious he would not submit to medical attention until he had given complete instructions as to the defence plan, had emphasized the absolute necessity of holding the position and had ordered his one remaining officer to take over.
By his calm courage, gallant conduct and total disregard for his own safety, he fired his men with grim determination and their firm stand enabled the regiment to accomplish its object of furnishing the brigade with a solid base through which to launch further successful attacks to clear the forest thus enabling the division to accomplish its task.
The final citation, Mr. Chairman, is that of Corporal Frederick George Topham, which reads as follows:
The king has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the Victoria Cross to:
B.39039 Corporal Frederick George Topham, 1st Canadian Parachute Battalion
On 24th March, 1945, Corporal Topham, a medical orderly, parachuted with his battalion onto a strongly defended area east of the Rhine. At about 1100 hours whilst treating casualties sustained in the drop, a cry for help came from a wounded man in the open. Two medical orderlies from a field ambulance went out to this man in succession but both were killed as they knelt beside the casualty.
Without hesitation and on his own initiative Corporal Topham went forward through intense fire to replace the orderlies who had been killed before his eyes. As he worked on the wounded man, he was himself shot through the nose. In spite of severe bleeding and intense pain be never faltered in his task. Having

Demobilization-Army
completed immediate first aid, he carried the wounded man steadily and slowly back through continuous fire to the shelter of the woods.
During the next two hours Corporal Topham refused all offers of medical help for his own wound. He worked most devotedly throughout this period to bring in wounded, showing complete disregard for the heavy and accurate enemy fire. It was only when all casualties had been cleared that he consented to his own wound being treated.
His immediate evacuation was ordered, but he. interceded so earnestly on his own behalf that he was eventually allowed to return to duty.
On his way back to his company he came across a carrier, which had received a direct hit. Enemy mortar bombs were still dropping around, the carrier itself was burning fiercely and its own mortar ammunition was exploding, an experienced officer on the spot had warned all not to approach the carrier.	-
Corporal Topham, however, immediately went out alone in spite of the blasting ammunition and enemy fire, and rescued the three occupants of the carrier. He brought these men back across the open and, although one died almost immediately afterwards, he arranged for the evacuation of the other two, who undoubtedly owe their lives to him.
This non-commissioned officer showed sustained gallantry of the highest order, for six hours, most of the time in great pain. He performed series of acts of outstanding bravery and his magnificent and selfless courage inspired all those who witnessed it.

At a more recent date, in 1943, it was my privilege to see the Regiment de Hull, which came from this immediate area, standing for hours in the waters of the Bering sea, unloading stores from the boats on to the island of Kiska; and on armistice day, in November, 1943, I spent that day in the tents of the Regiment de Hull. There was an arctic blizzard blowing and the instruments registered that gale as blowing at ninety miles an hour. One could hardly stand up against it. The freezing sleet would blow horizontally to the ground, and I say here, and nobody who was on that island could contradict me, that those French-Canadian ' soldiers of the Regiment de Hull were the life and soul of that garrison, be they Canadian or United States soldiers who were there.
Therefore when those French-Canadian soldiers who had been called up under the N.R.M.A. were appealed to last year to volunteer many of them had to wrestle between two loyalties, one loyalty that might be described as parental loyalty, a loyalty to their home and to their family, as against a loyalty to a cause which they barely understood. With regard to the decision to be made whether they should go back on promises they had made when they were first called up, promises to their parents that they would not volunteer for service outside Canada, whether that decision should be madeJ by them or by the government, they were unanimous in feeling that the decision should be made by the government and not by the individual man. No wonder those men placed the responsibility squarely upon the shoulders of the government. This man-power skeleton will remain long in the Liberal cupboard.
I suggest that even at this eleventh hour, in the interests of efficiency, for the wellbeing of the N.R.M.A. soldiers who are still here and for the sake of the unity of Canada, this two-army system be discontinued from now on.
Our soldiers are returning, but I suggest that the methods by which they are being repatriated are open to the severest condemnation because those men who have had the longest and hardest service, as the minister said to-day, are not having a fair chance in being returned; that men who have served a much shorter time overseas are now coming back, while many of the men who have had

the longest service still have to remain, not because they are in some particularly essential job, but because they do not happen to be in a formation which is being brought back, and because only lip-service is being given to this policy of "first in, first out; longest and hardest, first home."
The point system as described by the minister to-day is totally unjust to the man who has seen the longest and hardest fighting. Two points are allowed for service in Canada and only one additional point for service overseas. "Service overseas" does not mean overseas in a theatre of operation; it may mean service in a pleasant camp in England. The present point system should be revised immediately if fairness and justice are to be observed. That is very much the feeling of the men who are returning to Canada to-day. I have talked with men who have been repatriated to Ottawa with the Princess Louise Dragoon Guards, with men of the Hastings and Prince Edward regiment from Belleville, with men of the 48th battalion being demobilized in Toronto, and with men of the Seafortih Highlanders of Canada who passed through here a week ago on their way to Vancouver. These men who served with me in the first Canadian division in the early days of the war, some of whom I could recognize, many of whom were able to recognize me, were all loud in their protests against the unfair way in which the present point system is working, and the fact that included in. their ranks were men who had seen no fighting whatever. In the last session, the Minister of National Defence gave the information that by the 1st of March of this year, three and a half months before V-E day, only 238 N.R.M.A. soldiers had reached an actual battlefield. We hear now that a hundred and eleven chousand of our men have been repatriated. A return was tabled yesterday which gave some startling figures regarding the type of men who were in those units which are now being repatriated. I jotted down a few. Of the Saskatchewan Light Infantiy twenty-seven per cent are N.R.M.A. soldiers; of the Seaforths, 19-5 per cent; of the PJP.C.L.I., 18-5 per cent, and, with all but two of the infantry battalions which are back, more than ten per cent are N.R.M.A. soldiers. Compare those figures with the statement which was given by the minister last session, that by the 1st of March of this year only 238 N.R.M.A. men had reached the actual battlefield. Also compare that with the figures which were given earlier, which I mentioned, that there were over four thousand men in the army of occupation who had served for more than six months in an actual theatre of war.

United Nations Agreement
It is on these facts that I feel we must criticize, and criticize severely, the present point system by which these men are being brought back. Even at this eleventh hour it should be revised, and some additional bonus, some preference should be granted or some scheme devised-I care not how you work it out-for the benefit of the men who have been in actual combat and to whom the minister referred as having the hardest and longest service. Unless we want to pay more lip-service to that policy some action must be taken in that respect.
A short time ago disciplinary action was taken against an officer who was editing the Maple Leaf magazine at the time. But talk to any man who is coming back and he will tell you that those editorials reflect the opinion of the troops who then were actually in Germany or elsewhere on the continent of Europe.
I have confined myself in the main to criticism of the policy. I feel that not sufficient foresight is being used at this time in preparing our future defence forces so that they may assure reasonable and adequate defence of this country in another global war where we might be faced with an enemy equipped with the most scientific developments of this atomic age. We should think twice before we go back to the time-worn policies and time-worn formations which we had before this war.
I appeal that consideration be given to our army of occupation, and that some reasonable scheme of replacing those men who have served in the army of occupation for any extended period should be worked out now. No such scheme was presented to us.
Finally, I say that even now we must revise our repatriation scheme, so that those who have served the longest and fought the hardest may have the advantage of coming back and becoming reestablished in this country, or of taking some of the many courses which are being opened for them, before they find all those opportunities gone.
I have not made any comment on the various items of the establishment because I understand that an opportunity to discuss these in detail will be presented at a later date. I therefore move that the debate on this subject be adjourned.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
